tldr: A comprehensive survey categorizing roughly 150 verifiers essential for robot policy evaluation and learning into four judgment sources, formalizing the fundamental cost-vs-reliability trade-off: "No Free Checker."
hero_caption: Overview of learned and pretrained verifiers in robot learning. It summarizes three main use cases: evaluating behavior and policies (Section 4.1), test-time action selection and lookahead with world models (Section 4.2), and feeding feedback into reward optimization and data filtering (Section 4.3).
overview:
With the rise of LLMs, robotics is rapidly adopting Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and world models. However, unlike math or code, the physical world has no cheap, deterministic rules to decide success or failure. Real-world evaluation faces imperfect sensors, expensive real-robot rollouts, the need for early verdicts to prevent irreversible hardware damage, and continuous notions of progress and safety. To address these challenges, "verifiers" that score robot behavior have become essential.

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of roughly 150 verifier studies, categorizing them into four families based on who supplies the judgment: human verifiers, rule-based and formal verifiers, learned and pretrained verifiers, and model-intrinsic verifiers. It introduces two coordinate axes: "availability" (how cheap, early, and dense verdicts are) and "credibility" (how much a high score tells us about true task completion).

Analyzing existing methods across these axes reveals a fundamental trade-off: "No Free Checker." Making verdicts cheaper and more frequent lowers their credibility, while demanding high credibility causes costs to skyrocket. In particular, when verifiers are exposed to optimization as reinforcement learning rewards or runtime gates, policies exploit blind spots through reward hacking, breaking verifier credibility. The paper examines frameworks to validate verifiers themselves and proposes nine metrics to report, providing clear guidance for designing future robust verifiers.
contributions: Systematically categorized roughly 150 robot verifier papers across four families based on who supplies the judgment: human, rule-based and formal, learned and pretrained, and model-intrinsic verifiers.
Defined the evaluation axes of "availability" and "credibility," formalizing the irreversible trade-off rule that there is "No Free Checker."
Highlighted, both theoretically and empirically, the breakdown of calibration due to reward hacking and covariate shift when verifiers are exposed to policy optimization search.
Proposed nine standard reporting metrics (such as the transfer reward gain ratio against a held-out verifier panel) to make claims about verifiers checkable and comparable.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need Verifiers for Robot Policies Now?
sections.summary: As VLAs and world models scale up, verifiers have become crucial for data filtering, post-training rewards, and inference-time search. Because of physical-world challenges, an inherent trade-off exists between availability (cheap verdicts) and credibility (accurate verdicts).
sections.details:
In robot learning, verifier signals are needed across every stage: filtering large-scale pretraining datasets, providing reward signals for reinforcement learning (post-training), selecting among candidate actions at inference time, and evaluating rollouts in world-model simulations. This paper defines a "verifier" as any mechanism that takes context (observations, goals, language instructions) and a candidate policy behavior, and returns a score.

Building verifiers in the physical world is uniquely difficult for four reasons:
- Deciding whether a physical task succeeded is expensive due to sensor noise and partial observability.
- Real-robot rollouts consume physical time, making evaluation hard to scale.
- A single bad action can damage hardware, requiring early verdicts mid-process before task completion.
- Task progress, motion smoothness, and safety are continuous quantities that cannot be captured by binary success flags.

Organizing roughly 150 papers reveals four families based on who supplies the judgment: human, rule-based and formal, learned and pretrained, and model-intrinsic verifiers. The most important insight across them is "No Free Checker." As judgment moves closer to the model itself or cheap neural networks, verdicts become cheaper, earlier, and denser (higher availability), but the credibility that this score reflects true task success drops sharply.

sections.heading: The Most Accurate but Most Expensive Standard: Human Verifiers
sections.summary: Human verification offers highly credible labels that directly reflect task intent, but it is expensive and hard to query frequently. Humans serve four roles—pairwise comparisons, time-series scoring, interventions, and validating generated rollouts—acting as supervision for cheaper verifiers.
sections.details:
Human verifiers provide judgments closest to true task intent, but sharing the constraint of very high acquisition costs. Human verifiers generally take four forms:

### 2.1 Comparing Trajectories
Two trajectory segments are presented to a human for a pairwise choice of which is better. Beyond directly ranking policies via blind tests as in RoboArena, this is widely used as a supervisory signal to train reward models from preference data (e.g., PEBBLE, B-Pref), distilling human judgment into cheaper verifiers.

### 2.2 Scoring Trajectories
Humans assign continuous scores along the time axis for a single trajectory. In reward sketching, a representative approach, users manually draw a 0-to-1 task progress curve while watching an execution video. A dense reward model is then trained from this small set of curves.

### 2.3 Intervening During Execution
A human monitors robot execution and seizes control (intervenes) right before a failure to provide corrective actions. Approaches split into "human-gated" setups where humans step in voluntarily (HG-DAgger, HACO, Sirius, HIL-SERL) and "robot-gated" setups where the robot requests help based on policy uncertainty (ThriftyDAgger, AIM, Sirius-Fleet). Intervention data avoids hazards while populating the replay buffer with high-value corrective demonstrations.

### 2.4 Validating Generated Rollouts
Humans inspect video rollouts generated by world models to judge "outcome preservation"—whether the simulation yields the same outcome as executing on hardware. In GigaWorld-1, humans evaluate combined scores of task success and video fidelity. In VeoEval, humans verify that real-world failures are not falsely counted as successes in simulation. These judgments are also ultimately turned into training data for automated evaluators such as VLMs.

sections.heading: Mathematical Guarantees and Simulator Privileges: Rule-Based and Formal Verifiers
sections.summary: These methods score behaviors using pre-written rules, predicates, or mathematical models. In simulators with full state access, they are fast, cheap, and offer strong guarantees, but they remain brittle to real-world perceptual noise and violated assumptions.
sections.details:
Because they apply criteria defined before execution, rule-based and formal verifiers return scores deterministically without human involvement at test time. They divide into three groups based on input granularity:

### 3.1 Full-Trajectory Verification
- Signal Temporal Logic (STL): Quantifies specification margins as real-valued "satisfaction margins." For example, it measures how far a gripper kept clear of a height constraint. Works calibrate these margins with conformal prediction for early warnings (Lindemann et al.) or convert them into dense RL rewards (TGPO).
- Geometric Scoring: Approaches like RINSE score trajectory quality directly from geometry using spectral arc length (smoothness) and envelope distance (self-similarity), filtering demonstration data without needing external task definitions.
- Model-Written Rules: Approaches offload verification code writing to AI, such as Eureka (prompting LLMs with environment code to evolve reward functions) and Code-as-Monitor (synthesizing runtime spatio-temporal monitoring code).

### 3.2 Terminal-State Verification
Checks whether goal predicates are satisfied (0/1) at the end of an episode using ground-truth object poses in a simulator. This is widely used for success detection in benchmarks like LIBERO and CALVIN, filtering synthetic demonstrations in MimicGen, and providing sparse RL rewards via GRPO in SimpleVLA-RL and RIPT-VLA. However, it cannot be used directly on hardware where ground-truth poses are unavailable, and it is vulnerable to hacking where geometric conditions are met without true task completion.

### 3.3 Physical-Constraint Verification
Methods using control barrier functions (CBFs) to provide invariance certificates that mathematically prove and enforce safety set containment, or Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) checks verifying whether symbolic preconditions are physically executable. They guarantee absolute safety as long as the underlying model is accurate.

captions.F3: Taxonomy of rule-based and formal verifiers: trajectory-level STL and geometric scores (Section 3.1), simulator terminal goal predicate checks (Section 3.2), and physical constraint guarantees via control barrier functions (Section 3.3).

sections.heading: Rise of VLMs and Video Models: Learned and Pretrained Verifiers
sections.summary: Verifiers using neural network forward passes provide flexible, dense scoring. Spanning task-specific trained models to zero-shot general VLMs, they are widely adopted for evaluation, inference-time search, and policy learning feedback.
sections.details:
Because neural-network-based verifiers output scores directly from images, they are easy to deploy on real robots and offer high availability.

### 4.1 Evaluating Behavior and Policies
- Process-Level Evaluation: Assigns progress scores to each video frame. Methods include computing dense rewards from video feature distances (VIP, LIV), predicting stage-wise completion (Robo-Dopamine, ProcVLM), or extracting generation probabilities of specific tokens in VLMs (TOPReward).
- Trajectory-Level Evaluation: Takes an entire video after task completion to output success verdicts and failure diagnoses (RoboFAC, WorldEval). Others evaluate video-generation world models by jointly scoring visual realism and task completion (GigaWorld-1).

### 4.2 Inference-Time Verification
Evaluates and filters multiple candidate actions generated by a policy at test time. RoboMonkey shows that sampling perturbed candidate actions and ranking them with a verifier reduces errors following a power law with sample count. Other methods use world models for multi-step latent lookaheads (FOREWARN, Foresight), rejecting or correcting actions as soon as danger is detected.

### 4.3 Feeding Verifier Feedback into Policy Learning
- Reward Optimization: Updates policies directly using verifier scores as RL rewards or preference optimization losses (RECAP, GRAPE, VLA-RL).
- Rollout Filtering (Self-Improvement): The policy filters its own collected rollouts using verifiers (e.g., Demo-SCORE), keeping only passing data for subsequent training loops.
- Offline Data Filtering: Weights large pre-collected datasets (like Open X-Embodiment) using mutual information (DemInf), domain reweighting (Re-Mix), or estimated policy performance contributions (DataMIL) to improve learning efficiency.

sections.heading: Zero Added Cost with Hidden Traps: Model-Intrinsic Verifiers
sections.summary: These methods repurpose internal features and uncertainties already produced during policy or world-model inference as verification scores. While computationally cheap and offering the highest availability, they carry the fundamental limit of sharing the model's own blind spots.
sections.details:
Without requiring external verifiers, these methods repurpose internal signals from the running policy or world model. They are the cheapest to obtain, but credibility demands caution.

### 5.1 Policy-Based Self-Verification
- Runtime Failure Detection: SAFE extracts intermediate representations from VLA models, using lightweight linear classifiers to detect anomalies based on latent space separation between successes and failures. Sentinel monitors temporal action jitter, while FAILDetect calibrates conformal prediction thresholds purely on successful demonstrations to limit false positives.
- Pre-Execution Candidate Pruning: MG-Select measures action token probability shifts under masked image or text inputs, picking candidates most grounded in observations. TACO leverages latent feature familiarity (pseudo-counts).

### 5.2 Prediction-Based Outcome Verification
Verification using world models:
- Trajectory Likelihood: Uses likelihoods from video prediction models trained on expert data directly as rewards (VIPER).
- Latent Discrepancy: Compares predicted versus observed latent states to detect physical execution breakdowns zero-shot.
- Model Uncertainty: Penalizes policy rollouts using disagreement or variance across world-model ensembles (MOPO, AHEAD).
- Reachability Values: Applies Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis under predicted dynamics to detect states where failure is unavoidable regardless of future actions, triggering safety fallbacks beforehand.

### 5.3 Beyond Action Verification: Task Selection
Used to select training environments rather than actions. ACCEL uses policy value-function underestimation (value loss) as a signal of unmastered environments to curate curriculum tasks.

While offering the lowest cost, this family faces an inherent vulnerability: the model assigns high scores to failures it falsely believes are correct (unrecognized failure modes).

captions.F5: Structure of model-intrinsic verifiers: policy self-verification via internal latents and uncertainty (Section 5.1), prediction outcome verification using world model likelihoods and discrepancies (Section 5.2), and task selection driven by policy value loss (Section 5.3).

sections.heading: How Do We Validate the Verifier? Optimization and Hacking
sections.summary: Verifier errors cascade into data filtering, policy ranking, RL rewards, and runtime safety. Beyond agreement on static datasets, verifiers require rigorous evaluation that tests robustness against reward hacking and conformal calibration collapse under optimization.
sections.details:
Verifier mistakes corrupt training data and overrate bad policies. The literature currently tests verifiers in three ways:

### 6.1 Agreement Benchmarks on Static Rollouts
Measures how well verifier outputs match human labels on fixed datasets (e.g., TOPReward benchmark, RoboReward, OpenGVL). However, reporting single agreement rates leaves critical gaps:
- It hides human label noise and the balance of false positives vs. false negatives (RoboReward showed frequent severe false positives, marking tasks successful when drawers were never opened).
- Confidence intervals are rarely reported.
- Domain gaps between evaluation datasets: GE-Sim 2.0 reported an 8-point gap between accuracy measured on world-model rollouts versus real-world videos.

### 6.2 Policy-Trained Metric
Measures verifier quality by training a policy using the verifier as a reward or filter, evaluating the resulting policy's success. However, this is rarely done because training policies is computationally expensive.

### 6.3 Verifier Behavior Under Optimization (Search) and Reward Hacking
This section raises the strongest warning. Optimizing a policy to maximize verifier scores (via RL search) rapidly drives the policy toward the verifier's blind spots where it mistakenly gives high scores (Goodhart's Law / reward hacking).
- Conformal Calibration Collapse: Statistical safety thresholds calibrated via conformal prediction on static offline data break because policy optimization induces distribution shift (violating exchangeability), invalidating safety guarantees.
- Independent Verifier Panel: Studies should evaluate whether apparent training gains are genuine by measuring transfer reward gain $\Delta_{\mathrm{panel}} / \Delta_{\mathrm{proxy}}$ against an independent held-out verifier panel.

### 6.4 Nine Checkable Metrics for Verifiers
The paper proposes nine standard reporting metrics to make verifier claims verifiable (including false positive/negative rates on fixed sets, confidence intervals, explicit domain specifications, and transfer reward gain ratios under optimization).

sections.heading: Conclusion: The Robotics Frontier Beyond "No Free Checker"
sections.summary: Surveying roughly 150 robot verifiers leads to the conclusion that availability and credibility sit in a fundamental trade-off: "No Free Checker." Establishing verification foundations that combine low cost with high credibility is the central challenge for next-generation robot foundation models.
sections.details:
This survey analyzed roughly 150 robot policy verifiers across four families: human, rule-based and formal, learned and pretrained, and model-intrinsic verifiers.

Moving judgment closer to the model itself yields cheaper, denser signals (higher availability) and enables earlier interventions. But this comes at the expense of credibility—it becomes harder to guarantee that the signal reflects true task completion. In the physical world, high availability and high credibility cannot be obtained together for free; this is the core meaning of "No Free Checker."

While proposals for learned and model-intrinsic verifiers are proliferating, validating their own credibility remains inadequate. The field urgently needs robust verifier designs that survive policy optimization search and fair verification protocols built on independent held-out panels.

takeaways: Verifiers face a fundamental availability-credibility trade-off (No Free Checker); do not place blind trust in internal model signals or cheap VLM scores.
When verifiers are exposed to optimization (e.g., RL rewards or test-time filtering), high agreement on static datasets quickly collapses due to reward hacking.
Statistical safety guarantees like conformal prediction fail under policy optimization because covariate shift violates the underlying exchangeability assumption.
Rather than trusting simulator terminal predicates or VLM scores alone, evaluation protocols must audit true performance gains using independent held-out verifier panels.
limitations: As a survey paper, it does not include new empirical benchmark experiments directly evaluating all verifier families under identical conditions on a unified task or hardware platform.

While protocols like independent panel audits are proposed to evaluate reward hacking resistance under optimization, standardized adversarial verifier benchmarks shared across the community are not yet established.

While the paper underwent author review regarding completeness, literature counts, and interpretations, it leveraged LLMs for drafting and may not capture every latest development in the rapidly evolving VLA space.
